newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Euro set to revolutionise Eurobonds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Euro set to revolutionise Eurobonds.

text.p: The single European currency will revolutionise thinking in fast-paced Eurobond markets as credit risk takes centre stage and the importance of relative market value diminishes.

Bond issuance volumes will also surge from current levels in component currencies given the euro's assured position as the world's alternate reserve currency -- and one which may possibly challenge the dollar's pre-eminence early in the 21st century.
These are some of the conclusions reached by new issues specialists gearing up for the euro-Eurobond market.
At the moment investors looking at a new Eurobond issue, ask two questions. First, "Do we like the market?' then "Do we like the credit?'.
The answer to the first question primarily involves making a judgment on the currency. High coupon bonds can prove a poor investment if the currency weakens over the life of the deal.

"With a single currency domestic markets will disappear, relative market value goes out the window and the answer to the first question must be yes," said Tim Skeet, executive director of debt capital markets at Lehman Brothers International.
"Then we have a credit spread market and the answer to the second question becomes all important."
Robin Monroe-Davies, managing director at European credit rating agency IBCA, agrees. He says that under a single currency credit risk would be the only real differential for investors.

"Of course, say, unrated German firms will still be able to get cheap funding from German banks on name recognition. But if they want to broaden their base the first thing an investor will ask is "What is the rating?," Monroe-Davies said.
Canada and its provinces are often cited as the blueprint for the eurobond market, comprising issues from both sovereign and corporate borrowers.
"There are obvious difference between the provinces and so they trade at different spreads," said Robin Baldwin, a director at London Bond Broking. "But basically they are all in line".
Skeet at Lehman Brothers said euro-denominated German government paper -- euro Bunds -- would be the benchmark against which all other deals would be priced. RISING VOLUME

Syndicate managers say the euro's potential status as the world's second-largest reserve currency would inevitably draw in many more investors than the sum of its parts now attract. Borrowers would be quick to satisfy new demand, they said.
Eight countries at most -- France, Germany, Austria, Belgium, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands -- are expected to take part in the first stage of EMU in 1999.
One forex strategist in London said he had no doubt "the euro will be a tight fiscal unit in its early years but perhaps at the expense of the kind of growth we may see in America".

International bonds launched in those eight currencies in the first nine months of 1996 totalled $155 billion for a 30.5 percent share of the total market, according to figures from Capital DATA Bondware.
Dollar deals totalled $208 billion for a 40.8 percent market share, while the yen had 7.9 percent with $40 billion. The whole market was worth $509 billion.

Going into the next century, eastern European borrowers will find favour as investment managers seek yield given an expected price stability/low interest rate environment in the EU under economic and monetary union.
Analysts said a test for countries wanting to join the euro bloc will be how far their yield spreads versus euro government paper can tighten over time.

"European Union candidates from eastern and central Europe can demonstrate their readiness (to join the EU) by having bonds in euros at yield spreads little different from EU governments," said Graham Bishop, EU advisor at Salomon Brothers in London.
Dealers said the market would be willing to buy this paper initially because of its relatively higher yield.

"EMU would mean price stability. The logic of that is we will have low interest rates. So investment managers will be looking for extra bits of yield by taking extra risk," said an EMU analyst at a U.S. bank here." REMOVAL OF BOUNDARIES
The euro's effective removal of national boundaries will remove the blinkers from those European investors who stick with paper denominated in their own currency at present.
While Baldwin at London Bond Broking said many funds were already operating on a Europe-wide basis, Monroe-Davies at IBCA said currency was a formal barrier for many investors.
Skeet said: "Patriotism won't last long once investors see they can get a much better deal elsewhere."
Those better deals may well be large, liquid transactions which smaller, weaker credits would not be able to issue.
So borrowers from particular sectors may group together, first nationally and later on a pan-European scale, to issue the large, liquid instruments the market may demand, analysts say.
At the same time such a move would provide cheaper funding for those involved.

Seven German states launched the first such jumbo deal earlier this year, a four billion mark 10-year deal. Some years ago several small British breweries combined to launch a sterling bond which has been increased by small amounts since.

A treasury manager at one of Britain's largest building societies said: "It's an obvious idea for smaller societies to consider if EMU means a bigger entry level size for bond issues. They will certainly respond to what the market wants."
"(Longer term) it may also be a route for the bigger societies if they have an increased demand for funds."
On interbank competition, dealers said EMU could lead to a big consolidation in the Eurobond industry.
"No longer will European banks have protected home markets. (Investor) flows will overcome patriotism and it will all become a matter of relative credits," said Skeet at Lehman.
Other ideas being bandied about included companies bypassing the banking system and going directly to central markets and further expansion of the securitised market.
"Many innovations will be rearrangements of existing credit currently provided by the banking system or the insurance industry through direct loans or private placements," said one U.S. banker.
"I can see all these coming into the public market because the borrowers will feel they can get the best price there."
